Volunteers who are residents of the city; and member from the planning and zoning committee.
An alternate will be appointed to the tree committee in accordance with city ordinances. In addition, one representative shall be appointed who is a city employee; provided, however, that the city employee who is appointed shall be a nonvoting member of the tree committee.
(1) Duties and responsibilities. It shall be the duty of the tree committee to study, develop, and update a written plan for the disposition of trees and shrubs on public lands, and undeveloped land within the city limits. Upon completion of the written plan, the tree committee will review such plan annually and, each October, present a report to the mayor and council. The tree committee, when requested by the mayor and council, shall consider, investigate, make findings, report and recommend upon any special matter coming within the scope of its work.
It shall also be the duty of the tree committee to apply for Tree City USA status and, if such status is achieved, to provide guidance in order for the city to continue as a Tree City USA. The tree committee will be responsible for the yearly Arbor Day Celebration.
(2) Operation. The tree committee shall elect a chairperson and a secretary. The secretary shall maintain official minutes of all meetings and proceedings. The tree committee shall meet as often as is necessary but at least quarterly. Meetings shall be called and conducted in accordance with the state open meeting law and minutes shall be maintained in accordance with the state open records law. A majority of active members shall be a quorum for transaction of business.
(3) Funding. Funding for the tree plan shall be included as a line item in the city's annual budget. The city administrator is responsible for providing a detailed tree care plan and budget.
(d) Definitions. All words in these standards have their customary dictionary definitions except as specifically defined herein. The words "shall" and "must" are mandatory, and the words "may" and "should" are permissive.
Agent(s), designated or authorized means an individual or entity authorized to administer and enforce the standards set forth in this article.
Buildable area means the portion of a parcel of land where a building may be located and which shall contain enough square footage to meet the minimum required by the zoning district. That portion which is not located in the minimum setbacks, utility corridors, driveways, slopes to build streets, tee save areas, landscape strips, specimen tree areas, state water buffer, tributary buffers, zoning buffers, wetlands, storm water and sanitary sewer easements.
Buffer means:
State waters buffer. An area along the course of any state waters to be maintained in an undisturbed and natural condition.
Zoning buffer. A natural undisturbed portion of a lot, except for approved access and utility crossings, which is set aside to achieve a visual barrier between the use on the lot and adjacent lots and/or uses. Buffer is achieved with natural vegetation and must be replanted subject to the approval of the city arborist or his/her designated agent(s) when sparsely vegetated. Cleaning of undergrowth from a buffer is prohibited except when accomplished under the supervision of the city arborist or his/her designated agent(s).
Caliper means the standard for trunk measurements of nursery stocks. Caliper of the trunk shall be taken six inches above the ground for up to and including four-inch caliper size and 12 inches above the ground for larger sizes.
Cambium means tissue within the woody portion of trees and shrubs which gives rise to the woody water and nutrient conducting system and the energy substrate transport system in trees. Cambium growth activity results in a tree's radial development, i.e., increase in diameter.
Cambial dieback means the irreparable radial or vertical interruption of a tree's cambium, usually caused by mechanical damage, such as skinning bark or from excessive heat.
Clear cutting means the removal of all trees from a property, whether by cutting or other means, excluding stream buffer requirements.
Coniferous means belonging to the group of cone bearing evergreen trees and shrubs
City arborist means the agent(s) of the city having the primary responsibilities of administration and enforcement of this article. Such person shall be certified by the SIA.
Critical root zone means the area of tree roots within the crown dripline. This zone is generally defined as a circle with a radius extending from a tree's trunk to a point no less than the furthest crown dripline. Disturbances within this zone will directly affect a tree's chance for survival.
Crown drip line means a vertical line extending down to the ground from the end of the tree's longest branches.
Deciduous means not persistent; the shedding of leaves annually.
D.B.H. means diameter-at-breast-height is a standard measure of tree size (for trees existing on site) and is a tree trunk diameter measured in inches at a height of four and one-half feet above the ground. If a tree splits into multiple trunks below four and one-half feet, then the trunk is measured at its most narrow point beneath the SPL.
Improvement setback means an area adjacent to a zoning buffer in which no improvements and/or structures shall be constructed. No development activity such as tree removal, stump removal or grinding, land disturbance or grading is permitted without the approval of the city arborist.
Land development means the performance of any building or mining operation, the making of any material change in the use or appearance of any structure or land, the division of land into two or more parcels, and the creation or termination of rights of access or riparian rights.
Land disturbing activity means any activity, which may result in soil erosion from water or wind and movement of sediments into state water or onto lands within the state, including, but not limited to, clearing, dredging, grading, excavating, transporting, and filling of land but not including agricultural practices.
Land disturbance permit means a permit issued by the city that authorizes the commencement of alteration or development of a given tract of land or the commencement of any land disturbing activity.
Landscape plan means a plan that identifies areas of tree preservation and methods of tree protection within the protected zone, as well as all areas of replanting. Within replanting areas, the common and botanical names of the proposed species, the number of plants of each species, the size of all plant materials, the proposed location of all plant materials, and any unique features of the plant materials shall be indicated.
Landscape strip means an area required by this article by any condition of zoning, use permit or variance approval, which is reserved for the installation and/or maintenance of plant materials.
Minimum setback means the minimum yards as specified in the regulations related to the zoning districts or use permit categories. A minimum required space between a property line and a structure. An area defined by a building line.
Protected zone includes but is not limited to the following:
(1) Critical root zone plus an additional three feet;
(2) All areas of a parcel required to remain in undisturbed open space;
(3) All areas required as landscape strips and/or buffers;
(4) Tree save areas according to city ordinances, conditions of zoning, use permit or variance approval, and/or this article.
Re-vegetation means the replacement of trees and landscape plant materials to satisfy the minimum tree density and landscape requirements, as determined by the city ordinances, condition of zoning, use permit or variance approval, or this article.
Roots means:
(1) Feeder roots. A complex system of small annual roots growing outward and predominantly upward from the system of "transport roots." These roots branch four or more times to form fans or mats of thousands of fine, short, non-woody tips. Many of these small roots and their multiple tips are two-tenths to one-millimeter or less in diameter and less than one to two millimeters long. These roots constitute the major fraction of a tree's root system surface area and are the primary sites of absorption of water and nutrients
(2) Major woody roots. First order of tree roots originating at the "root collar" and growing horizontally in the soil to a distance of between three and 15 feet from the tree's trunk. These roots branch and decrease in diameter to give rise to "rope roots." The primary functions of major woody roots include anchorage, structural support, the storage of food reserves, and the transport of minerals and nutrients.
(3) Rope roots. An extensive network of woody second order roots arising from major woody roots, occurring within the surface 12 to 18 inches of local soils, and with an average size ranging from one-quarter to one-inch in diameter. The primary function of rope roots is the transport of water and nutrients and the storage of food reserves.
(4) Transport roots. The system or framework of tree roots comprised of major woody roots and rope roots.
Root collar means the point of attachment of major woody roots to the tree trunk, usually at or near the ground line and associated with a marked swelling of the tree trunk.
Root respiration means an active process occurring throughout the feeder root system of trees and involving the consumption of oxygen and sugars with the release of energy and carbon dioxide. Root respiration facilitates the uptake and transport of minerals and nutrients essential for tree survival.
Setback means a space between a property line and the line to which a building or specified structure may be constructed.
Soil compaction means a change in soil physical properties, which includes an increase in soil weight per unit volume and a decrease in soil pore space. Soil compaction is caused by repeated vibrations, frequent traffic and weight. As related to tree roots, compacted soil can cause physical root damage, a decrease in soil oxygen levels with an increase in toxic gasses, and can be impervious to new root development.
State waters means any and all rivers, streams, creeks, branches, lakes, reservoirs, ponds, drainage systems, springs, wells, and other bodies of surface or subsurface water, natural or artificial, lying within or forming a part of the boundaries of the state which are not entirely confined and retained completely upon the property of a single individual, partnership, or corporation.
Thinning means selective cutting or removal of timber. A minimum of 80 D.B.H. per acre must remain.
Timber harvesting means the felling of timber products (pulp wood, etc.). The term "timber harvesting" may include both clear cutting and thinning of timber.
Tree means:
Tree. Any self-supporting woody perennial plant, which has a trunk diameter of two inches or more measured at a point six inches above the ground level and which normally obtains a height of at least ten feet at maturity, usually with one main stem or trunk and many branches.
Heritage tree. A tree, which is designated upon approval by the tree committee or authorized agent(s) to be of notable historical value or interest because of its age, size, or historical association.
Specimen tree. Any tree, which has been determined by the city arborist to be of high value because of its type, size, age, or other professional criteria, and has been so designated according to administrative standards established by the city council.
Stand of specimen trees. A contiguous grouping of trees which has been determined to be of value by the city arborist or authorized designee(s).
(1) A relatively mature even-aged stand.
(2) A stand with purity of species composition or of a rare or unusual nature.
(3) A stand of historical significance.
(4) A stand with exceptional aesthetic quality.
Tree preservation ordinance means the ordinance from which this article is derived, approved and adopted by the city council to provide standards for the protection, preservation and replacement of trees regulated and enforced by the city arborist in conjunction with the planning and zoning committee or designated agent(s) through development and construction permits and processes.
Tree protection plan or TPP means a plan to be submitted as part of the land disturbance process. This plan will include tree protection details, spatial limits, and implementation schedule as outlined in section 30-102 and appendices.
Tree save area means all areas designated for the purpose of meeting tree density requirements, saving specimen trees, and/or preserving natural buffers.
Tributary means any perennial stream (or portion thereof) within the affected area that is portrayed as a solid blue line on the United States Geological Survey 7.5 Quadrangle Maps, 1968 edition, or other perennial streams as identified by the city.
Wetlands means those areas that are inundated or saturated by surface or ground water at a frequency and duration sufficient to support, and that under normal circumstances do support, a prevalence of vegetation typically adapted for life in saturated soil conditions. Wetlands generally include swamps, marshes, bogs, and similar areas.
Zoning regulations means the zoning resolution of the city as amended or such regulations subsequently adopted by the city council inclusive of conditions of zoning, use permit or variance approval established pursuant thereto.
All other terms. All other words or phrases as appropriate to the context of their uses shall be interpreted as defined in the zoning regulations.
(e) Permit procedures.
(1) All applications for a land disturbance permit shall provide a tree protection plan and other documentation as required and as applicable for all areas of the tract of land within a protected zone. All applications and required supplemental information shall be submitted to city hall. [The tree protection plan may be separate from or included with the landscape plan.]
(2) All tree protection plans (TPP) and related documentation shall be reviewed by the city arborist for conformance to the provisions of these regulations and either approved, returned, for revisions, or denied within 30 days of receipt. If denied or returned for revisions the reasons for denial or revision shall be annotated on the TPP or stated in writing.
(3) Issuance of a valid land disturbance permit shall constitute an approval of the required tree protection plan and shall indicate conformance to the provisions of these regulations.
(4) For issuance of any residential building permit, applicants must sign and agree to abide by the residential erosion and sedimentation control tree protection agreement, (see appendices to section 30-102).
(5) For issuance of a timber harvesting permit, applicant agrees to maintain a 25-foot undisturbed buffer along the entire perimeter of the property. This buffer must be maintained for the duration of the timber harvesting activity.
(f) Removal of tree(s).
(1) If the owner/developer proposes to remove any tree(s) in the protected zone, then the owner/developer must document a hardship such as but not limited to economic or zoning restrictions and submit it as part of the application for a land disturbance permit. The application shall be subject to the approval of the city arborist or designated agent before any trees are to be removed from the site. Nothing in these regulations shall be construed to allow the removal of vegetation in a natural, undisturbed buffer required by the zoning regulations.
(2) When no trees are present in the protected zone or when disturbance of any portion of the protected zone is approved, it shall be the responsibility of the owner/developer to re-vegetate said areas (in which improvements are not constructed) with trees or other plant materials subject to zoning regulations or, in lieu thereof, administrative standards.
(3) Not withstanding any of the other requirements of these regulations, it shall be unlawful to remove a specimen tree without the express written consent of the city arborist or authorized agent(s). Administrative standards have been established for the identification, preservation and protection of specimen trees.
(4) The city arborist or designated agent shall approve an application for the removal of a protected or specimen tree provided at least one of the following conditions are met:
• The location of the tree prevents the opening of reasonable and necessary vehicular traffic lanes;
• The location of the tree prevents the construction of utility lines or drainage facilities, which may not be feasibly relocated;
• The location of the tree prevents reasonable access to the property, if no alternative access exists;
• Allowing the tree to remain would impose an economic burden upon the owner of the property entirely out of proportion to with the benefit gained by retaining the tree;
• The tree is diseased, dead or dying to the point that repair or restoration is not practical or the disease may be transmitted to other trees;
• There is no reasonable assurance that if the tree is saved with proper construction precautions, it will continue to live as an asset to the site.
(g) Violations. Citations for any of the following violations, by authorized city enforcement agent(s) may constitute issuance of an immediate stop work order:
(1) Land disturbance and/or tree removal within state water, tributary, or zoning buffer(s).
(2) Land disturbance and/or tree removal within tree save area(s).
(3) Illegal removal or disturbance of specimen tree, heritage trees or stands of trees.
(4) Improper installation of tree fencing.
(5) Other violations of any provision(s) of this article established pursuant thereto, including appendices.
(h) Enforcement. It shall be the duty of the city administrator or designated agent(s) to enforce this article. The city administrator or designated agent(s) shall have the authority to modify, revoke, suspend, or void any land disturbance permit and shall have the authority to suspend all work on a site or any portion thereof.
The city administrator or designated agent(s) is the issuing authority and shall have the power to withhold all permits, including, but not limited to, final certificates of occupancy, building permits and all permits on the subject site until it is determined by the issuing authority that the site complies with this article and the provisions of the formal plan approved by the county.
(i) Inspections. The city arborist is the issuing authority and may cause inspection of compliance to be made periodically by it's designated agent(s) during the course of the project and shall make a final inspection following the completion of the work. Applicants shall cooperate with the issuing authority in conducting such inspections.
The city arborist shall have the power to conduct such investigations as it may reasonably deem necessary to carry out its duties as prescribed in this article, including but not limited to the power to enter at reasonable times upon any property, public or private, for the purpose of investigating and inspecting the sites of any land disturbing or tree removal activities.
The city administrator is authorized to design and implement an inspection program involving private inspectors acceptable to the department.
No person shall refuse entry or access to any authorized representative or agent who requests entry for the purpose of inspection and who presents appropriate identification, nor shall any person obstruct, hamper or interfere with any such representative while in the process of carrying out his official duties.
(j) Notice of violation. If, through inspection, it is determined that a person, firm, or corporation has:
(1) Engaged in land disturbing or other activities, which have resulted in the removal of trees; or
(2) Failed to comply with the terms and conditions of a validly issued permit, then a written notice of violation shall be served upon the property owner or the agent of record.
Where a person, firm, or corporation has engaged in land disturbing or tree removal activities without having first secured a permit therefore in violation of this article, notices under the provisions of this article may be served upon the person in charge or any person representing the person in charge on the site. All construction and land disturbance activity shall be discontinued until the necessary measures to achieve compliance have been fulfilled.
The notice shall set forth the measures necessary to achieve compliance with the permit and shall state the time within which such measures must be completed
If the person, firm, or corporation engaged in land-disturbing activity fails to comply within the time specified, he/she shall be subject to citation for violation of this article.
(k) Stop work orders.
(1) Upon notice from the city administrator, work on any project that is being done contrary to the provision of this article shall be immediately stopped, until such time that the violation has been remedied to the satisfaction of the city manager. Prior to re-mediation a plan shall be submitted to and approved by the city arborist.
(2) Such notice.
a. Shall be in writing.
b. Shall state the specific violations.
c. Shall be given to the applicant, owner, the authorized agent of either, or the person in charge, or any person representing the person in charge of the activity on the subject property.
d. Shall state the conditions under which work may be resumed. Where an emergency exists, no written notice shall be required.
e. Shall allow only erosion control work to continue while stop work is in effect.
(l) Modification, revocation, suspension, voidance of permit. A land disturbance permit and/or other permit(s) required by this article may be modified, revoked, suspended, or voided by the city arborist upon finding that the holder is in violation of the terms of the permit or any portion of this article.
(m) Bonding. The city will evaluate all development projects (excluding timber harvesting) requesting property clear cutting. If upon completion of the site evaluation, the city arborist deems it appropriate to allow property clear cutting activities; a bond will be required. The bond will be required by the city as a mechanism to cover any potential cost associated with re-vegetation of the clear-cut property in the event of property abandonment.
The required bond amount will be 100 percent of the total cost for replanting trees to satisfy the density standards for the project site. A tree replacement cost obtained from a plant nursery will be provided to the city with the clear-cut request and the bond amount will be based on the tree replacement cost, the city reserves the right to request additional replacement cost if deemed appropriate. The city will hold the bond until the project activity, including tree replacement to satisfy the site density requirements, is completed. If upon issuing the land disturbance permit, the property is clear-cut and there are no construction or development activities conducted within six months, the city will attempt to contact the property owner (via certified mail) for a project update. Should the property owner not respond within 30 days of receipt of the status request, the bond will be used to re-vegetate the project site.
(n) Fines and penalties. Any person, firm, corporation or other entity violating any of the provisions of this article shall be liable for a fine of up to a maximum $1,000.00 per violation per day. Each calendar day a violation exists shall be considered a separate offense. There are no maximum limitations to the accrual of fines. Each owner of any property wherein a violation exists shall be jointly and severally responsible for said violations.
(o) Appeals. Any person aggrieved or affected by any decision of the city arborist relating to the application of these regulations may file an appeal within 30 days of the decision with the city council for relief or reconsideration. Appeals shall only be granted for errors of interpretation or where the unique natural features of the site are such that application of these regulations would create an undue hardship to the property owner, and in other instances where an undue hardship is created for the owner of the property.

(5) Tree protection. Standards for specimen and heritage trees and stands of trees:
Specimen and heritage tree. Any tree in fair or better condition which equals or exceeds the following diameter sizes:
Tree Type | Tree Diameter Size | Examples
Large Hardwoods | 25" d.b.h. | Oak, Hickory, Yellow Poplar, Sweetgum, Beech, etc.
Large Softwoods | 26" d.b.h. | Pine, Deodar Cedar
Small Native Flowering | 8" d.b.h. | Dogwood, Redbud, Sourwood
A tree in fair or better condition must meet the following minimum standards:
• A life expectancy of greater than ten years.
• A relatively sound and solid trunk with no extensive decay or hollow, and less than 20 percent radial trunk dieback.
• No more than one major and several minor dead limbs (hardwoods only).
• No major insect or pathological problem.
• A lesser-sized tree can be considered a specimen if it is a rare or unusual species, of exceptional quality, or of historical significance.
• A lesser size tree can be considered a specimen tree if it is specifically used by a builder, developer, or design professional as a focal point in a project or landscape.
Specimen tree stands. A contiguous grouping of trees which has been determined to be of value by the city's authorized agent(s). Determination is based upon one of the following criteria:
• A mature even-aged stand.
• A stand with purity of species composition or of a rare or unusual nature.
• A stand of historical significance.
• A stand with exceptional aesthetic quality.
(b) Methods of tree protection.
(1) Planning consideration. Tree space is the most critical factor in tree protection throughout the development process. The root system of trees can easily go beyond the dripline of the tree canopy. The root system within the dripline region is generally considered to be the critical root zone. Disturbance within this zone can directly affect a tree's chances for survival. To protect these critical root zones the following standards shall apply:
• The protective zone of specimen trees, heritage trees, stands of trees or otherwise designated tree save areas shall include no less that the total area beneath the tree(s) canopy as defined by the farthest canopy of the tree(s) plus a minimum of three additional feet. In some instances, the city arborist or authorized agent(s) may require a protective zone up to ten feet outside the dripline area. (See appendix A—Typical critical root zone.)
• Layout of the project site utility and grading plans must accommodate the required tree protective zones. Utilities must be placed along corridors between protective zones.
• Construction site activities such as parking, material storage, bury pits, concrete washout, burn hole placement, etc., shall not be allowed within tree protection zones.
• No disturbance shall occur within the protective zone of tree save areas.
(2) Protective barriers. Protective tree fencing shall be installed along the outer edge of and completely surrounding the critical root zones, plus a minimum of three additional feet of all specimen trees, heritage trees, stands of trees, or otherwise designated tree protective zones, prior to any land disturbance. Acceptable tree fencing procedures:
• A minimum of four feet high, constructed in a post and rail configuration. A two-inch by four-inch post and a double one-inch by four-inch rail is recommended.
• Four-foot orange polyethylene laminar safety fencing.
• Any deviation from the requirements listed above must be authorized by the city arborist or designated agent(s).
• All tree protection fences must be accompanied by "keep out" or "tree save" signage.
• All tree protection zones shall be designated as such with "tree save area" signs posted visibly on exterior sides of the fenced in area. These signs are intended to inform subcontractors of the tree protection process. Signs requiring subcontractor compliance with tree protection standards are required at all site entrances.
• A stop work order or notice of violation will issued if project is found to be out of compliance with the tree protection/landscape plan. A copy of the approved tree protection/landscape plan shall be attached to all building permits to be checked by each inspector (building, electrical, plumbing, etc.)
• All specimen trees, heritage trees, stands of trees or otherwise designated tree protection zones must be protected from silt.
Silt fencing reinforced with wire mesh fencing must be placed along the outer uphill edge of tree protective zones at the land disturbance interface.
Silt fencing should be backed by 12 gauge, two-inch by four-inch wire mesh fencing in areas of steep slope. (Steep slopes are defined at greater than 3H:IV).
All erosion control measures must comply with city standards.
• All tree fencing and erosion control barriers must be installed prior to and maintained throughout the land disturbance process and building construction and may not be removed until certificate of occupancy is issued, and approved by the city administrator or designated agent(s).
(3) Re-vegetation—Tree replacement.
a. The replacement of trees to satisfy the conditions of zoning, or this article, shall occur under the following conditions:
• To establish the minimum tree density requirements for the site.
• Where grading occurs outside the buildable portion of the lot.
• If the lot's buildable area leaves no protected zone.
• If no trees are present within an existing zone.
• Where specimen trees or stands of trees within the buildable portion of the lot are to be removed.
• Where specimen trees or stands of trees and trees within otherwise designated protective zones have been irreparably damaged or removed through land disturbance or construction activities.
b. The spacing of replacement trees must be compatible with special limitations and with responsible consideration towards potential species size. The following criteria shall be used to determine which trees are to be retained, removed and where trees are to be located for replacement:
POSITIVE CRITERIA:
• A species that is long-lived;
• A species that is native to the area;
• The hardiness of the tree;
• A low incidence of exfoliating bark, branch drop, and pruning;
• The protection of buildings from wind, sun, and other climatic considerations. The encouragement of wildlife residence;
• The suitability of size and maturity to the tree's function;
• The ability to retain soil and erosion;
• The ability to reduce noise;
• Draught resistant.
NEGATIVE CRITERIA:
• Susceptibility to insect and disease attack and to air and water pollution;

In order to maintain and enhance aesthetic standards in the city, the city has determined that buffer standards need to be adopted and enforced along its community collector roads. These roads are Rockaway Road, Highway 16, Highway 85, Stallings Road from city line to Matthews Street, Pylant Road from city line to Clarke's Street, Rockhouse Road, and Luther Bailey Road.
Other benefits associated with these regulations are:
• Enhanced property values.
• Reduced soil erosion, storm-water management costs and flooding potential.
• Moderation of microclimates.
• Improved air and water quality.
• Mitigation of noise and glare.
• Energy conservation through reduced heating and cooling.
The following buffer standards shall apply to all residential and nonresidential development along these highways:
(A) Residential buffers. A continuous 60-foot-wide (minimum) greenbelt buffer shall be preserved or established for any residential development adjacent to a collector road. The natural tree/landscape is to be preserved wherever possible.
(B) Nonresidential buffers. A continuous 50-foot-wide tree-save/landscape buffer shall be preserved or established for any nonresidential development adjacent to an arterial highway. The natural vegetation is to be preserved wherever possible.

APPENDIX G. TREE AND SITE RELATED DISTURBANCES
Tree protection zones, specimen trees or stands of trees designated to be saved must be protected from the following damages which may occur during all phases of land disturbance and construction processes, Methods of tree protection and disturbance prevention are provided in section 30-101(b)(2).
• Direct physical root damage.
• Indirect root damage.
• Trunk and crown disturbances.
A. Direct physical root damage most frequently occurs during site clearing and grading operations, where transport or feeder roots are cut, torn, or removed.
1. Transport and feeder roots tend to tangle and fuse among the roots of adjacent trees. The removal of trees with heavy machinery along the outer periphery of a tree save area can result in considerable damage within the tree save area.
2. The most substantial form of root damage for all root types occurs in the form of cut roots. Roots are cut in grade reduction or from trenching for underground utilities, sanitary sewer, or storm sewer lines.
3. A more subtle form of root damage is the loss of feeder roots. Feeder roots normally occur within the organic layer and the surface four inches of topsoil, subsequently, these roots can be easily damaged by the track action from a single bulldozer pass. The stripping of topsoil within a tree's critical root zone can totally eliminate its feeder root system.
B. Indirect root damage through site modification can result from positive grade changes, temporary storage of fill material, sedimentation of erosion materials, soil compaction, and soil chemical changes.
• Positive grade changes from fill and sedimentation causes a decrease in soil oxygen levels. An increase in soil carbon dioxide and other toxic gases can also occur, leading to large areas of anaerobic soil conditions and causing a decrease in the root respiration process, which is essential for the uptake and transport of mineral and nutrients.
• Anaerobic soil conditions are also produced by soil compaction, the increase in soil bulk density with a decrease in soil pore space. Compacted soil is also impervious to root penetration, and thus inhibits root development. Soil compaction is generally caused by the weight and vibrations of heavy machinery, vehicle parking, and the storage of fill and/or construction material within the critical root zones of trees.
• Changes in soil chemistry will adversely affect tree survival. The most frequent occurrence is the change (decrease) in soil acidity by concrete washout. Most trees native to the county area prefer slightly acid soils; concrete residues are highly basic. The leakage or spillage of toxic material such as fuels or paints can be fatal for trees.
C. Trunk and crown disturbance are generally mechanical in nature and are either caused directly by clearing and grading machinery, or indirectly by debris being cleared and falling into trees marked for protection.
• Common forms of damage include stripped bark and cambium, split trunks, and broken limbs.
• Damage also occurs for the posting of signs such as building permits or survey markers on trees.
• Indirect damage can be caused by the placement of burn holes of debris fires too close to trees. The possible range of damage includes scorched trunks with some cambial dieback, the loss of foliage due to evaporative heat stress (leaf desiccation), and completely burned trunk and crowns.

BASIC CONSIDERATIONS FOR OPEN SPACE DESIGN GUIDELINES
1. Set aside ridgelines, steep slopes, flood prone areas, wetlands, significant natural features, and historic and archaeological resources as a core for open space. Take care to ensure that the resulting configuration is coherent and reasonably contiguous. Whenever possible, arrange open space to abut existing or potential open space on adjoining properties. Map D displays topographical features that should be conserved, while Map E shows cultural, historic, and archaeological resources.
2. Site buildings in harmony with landforms. Locate new buildings and structures where neither construction nor access causes substantial alteration to topography or natural resources.
3. Take advantage of existing topography to preserve the lay of the land. Fit buildings and other amenities in to the site. Use slopes advantageously to accommodate multilevel structures with entrances on more than one level (e.g. walk out basements, garages under houses). Reserve flatter areas for septic fields and parking. Use natural landforms to screen structures from public roads. Map F illustrates how a natural feature such as a hill can protect a viewshed by screening new construction from view of a country road.
4. Do not make large cuts in hillsides or grade large areas flat. Both practices can cause erosion and disrupt natural drainage patterns in addition to being ugly. Site buildings to avoid substantial modification to natural landforms.
5. Situate new construction to minimize disruption of traditional viewsheds. Loss of traditional viewscapes results in erosion of local sense of place. Progressive destruction of community character will result in the loss of any sense that one place is distinct from another place.
6. Set buildings back into or against tree lines to lessen the impact to the viewshed. New construction isolated in a field can destroy traditional atmosphere. Tree lines and other vegetative backdrops have a certain ability to absorb disruptive impacts on the landscape. Map G shows some house sites set back into the woods to prevent their intrusion into the viewshed.
7. Do not site buildings in open fields. If greater constraints apply to the rest of the parcel, locate buildings at the farthest edges of the fields, as seen from public roads. Map H shows two illustrations of this principle.
8. Take advantage of open fields as sites for septic tanks and fields. These uses are non-disruptive of traditional appearance.
9. Maintain existing tree lines and field edges, including irregular configurations. These features define outdoor space in traditional ways, and add variety and interest to viewsheds. Map I points out the kind of edges that should be conserved.
10. Use existing vegetation and topography to buffer and screen new construction from public roads. Viewsheds are protected, and housing is shielded from read noise and the gaze of the curious.
11. Plant traditional species and maintain traditional planting patterns. Communities that have developed over time generally have established planting practices. Ensure that new species harmonize with existing vegetation. Map J shows how new plantings of traditional species can lessen the impact of development on a viewshed by screening new construction from a country road.
12. Use existing roads whenever possible to minimize clearing and landscape destruction. Map K points out old alignments that can serve new development.
13. Widen existing roads as little as possible to take advantage of existing vegetation as a buffer. In addition, conventional wide, clear cut rights of way translate as super highway as opposed to rural.
14. Construct new roads as narrow as possible to maintain a rural atmosphere and avoid a discordant expressway atmosphere.
15. Do not run roads through the middle of open fields. Lessen the impact of a new road on a viewshed by placing it along tree lines or other landscape boundaries. Map L shows some applications of this principle.
